title: The Work-Energy Theorem
short: The net work done on an object equals its change in kinetic energy.
trouble: Students use the work of one force instead of the work of the net force.

blocks.html: Kinetic Energy is $K = \tfrac12 mv^2$. Work by a Constant Force says how much a force adds or removes. Put them together and you get one of the most useful shortcuts in mechanics.

The net work done on an object equals its change in kinetic energy: $\role[net work]{energy}{W_{net}} = \role[change in kinetic energy]{energy}{\Delta K} = \tfrac12 \role{mass}{m}\role[final speed]{velocity}{v_f}^2 - \tfrac12 \role{mass}{m}\role[initial speed]{velocity}{v_i}^2$. $W_{net}$ is the sum of the work done by every force, which equals the work done by the net force.

For a constant net force along the motion, $W_{net} = F_{net}\,d = ma\,d$. From motion without the time, $a\,d = \tfrac12(v_f^2 - v_i^2)$. Multiply by $m$: $W_{net} = \tfrac12 mv_f^2 - \tfrac12 mv_i^2$. So kinetic energy is exactly the quantity that the net work changes, and the theorem holds for changing forces too (add up the work in small steps).

blocks.name: ph-energy
blocks.cap: A box sliding to a stop: friction does negative work, and the kinetic energy bar shrinks by exactly that much.

blocks.title: Speed from work
blocks.q: A net work of $400\ \text{J}$ is done on a $50\ \text{kg}$ cart that starts from rest. How fast does it end up?

blocks.title: Braking force
blocks.q: A $1{,}200\ \text{kg}$ car moving at $20\ \text{m/s}$ stops in $50\ \text{m}$. Find the average braking force.

blocks.title: Several forces
blocks.q: A $10\ \text{kg}$ box at rest is pushed $5\ \text{m}$ with $40\ \text{N}$ while friction of $15\ \text{N}$ acts. Find its final speed.
steps: $W_{push} = 200\ \text{J}$, $W_{friction} = -75\ \text{J}$; gravity and the normal force do none.

blocks.html: The theorem is often the fastest route when a problem gives forces and distances but asks for a speed, with no time involved.

Using the work of one force (usually the push) instead of the net work. The push adds energy but friction takes some away, so the push alone overstates the gain in kinetic energy. Check: list every force, find each one's work with its sign, and add them before setting the total equal to $\Delta K$.
